title: Analytics Engineering and dbt
description: Master Analytics Engineering, modular SQL modeling, dbt Core and v2, materializations (view, table, incremental, ephemeral), SCD Type 2 snapshots, seeds, generic & singular data tests, Jinja macros, Slim CI/CD, and production pipeline orchestration.

quiz.q: What is the primary objective of Analytics Engineering and dbt in the modern data stack?
options: To replace transactional operational databases like PostgreSQL
To transform, model, test, and document raw warehouse data into clean, business-ready analytical datasets using modular SQL and software engineering best practices
To ingest binary log events directly from Apache Kafka
To build machine learning neural networks in Python
quiz.expl: Analytics Engineering bridges data engineering and data analytics by using dbt to transform already-loaded data in the warehouse into reliable, tested, and documented business datasets.

quiz.q: How does dbt execute transformations against a data warehouse?
options: It pulls all data to the local machine, transforms it in Python memory, and re-uploads it
It compiles Jinja-templated SQL files into platform-specific SQL queries and sends them to the connected warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, PostgreSQL) to execute in-place
It translates SQL models into C++ shared libraries
It uses MapReduce on a private Hadoop cluster
quiz.expl: dbt does not store data or process compute itself; it compiles SQL/Jinja and pushes execution directly down to the target data platform via adapters.

quiz.q: What is the difference between source() and ref() in a dbt model?
options: source() references raw tables loaded outside dbt, while ref() references other models within the dbt project and automatically builds the dependency graph
source() is for views, while ref() is for physical tables
source() runs only in production, while ref() runs in development
They are identical aliases
quiz.expl: source() declares external raw ingestion tables and enables freshness testing; ref() links dbt models together, enabling automatic DAG lineage and parallel execution.

quiz.q: What happens when a dbt model is configured with materialized='view'?
options: dbt creates a physical table in storage with all rows copied
dbt creates or replaces a SQL view definition in the warehouse, requiring zero extra storage but executing the underlying query on demand
dbt exports the query results as a CSV seed file
dbt stores the table in an in-memory Redis cache
quiz.expl: Views store only the SQL query definition in the database metadata; rows are evaluated dynamically when queried, minimizing storage at the cost of compute on read.

quiz.q: Why is an incremental model (materialized='incremental') useful for large transaction datasets?
options: It compresses data using gzip
It processes only new or modified rows since the last execution rather than rebuilding hundreds of millions of historical rows every run
It disables data testing to run faster
It converts SQL queries into Apache Spark jobs
quiz.expl: Incremental models use is_incremental() filters (e.g. updated_at > max(updated_at)) and unique keys to insert/update only changed records, saving massive warehouse compute.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the unique_key configuration in an incremental model?
options: It creates a unique index on the column in PostgreSQL
It tells dbt which column(s) to use for matching and updating existing records (e.g. in a MERGE statement) to prevent duplicate rows on re-execution
It encrypts the column using SHA-256
It deletes all NULL values from the table
quiz.expl: unique_key tells update-based strategies (like MERGE or delete+insert) how to match incoming records against existing warehouse rows to ensure idempotency.

quiz.q: What are the four built-in generic data tests provided by dbt Core?
options: sum, avg, min, max
unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships
is_positive, is_negative, is_zero, is_null
select, insert, update, delete
quiz.expl: dbt Core comes with four foundational generic assertions: unique (no duplicates), not_null (no nulls), accepted_values (enumerated domain list), and relationships (referential integrity).

quiz.q: When does a dbt data test pass?
options: When the test query returns more than 100 rows
When the test query returns exactly 0 rows (zero failing records)
When the database administrator approves it
When the execution time is under 1 second
quiz.expl: dbt tests are written as assertions that seek failing records; returning 0 rows indicates zero rule violations, so the test passes.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a generic test and a singular test in dbt?
options: Generic tests are defined once and parameterized in YAML across multiple models/columns; singular tests are standalone SQL queries asserting a specific business rule
Generic tests are for tables; singular tests are for views
Generic tests can only test strings; singular tests can test numbers
There is no difference
quiz.expl: Generic tests are reusable templates applied in schema YAML; singular tests are single SQL scripts located in the tests/ directory representing custom domain logic.

quiz.q: In dbt Snapshots, what type of dimensional tracking is implemented?
options: SCD Type 0 (Fixed values)
SCD Type 1 (Overwriting existing values)
SCD Type 2 (Tracking historical versions with validity windows dbt_valid_from and dbt_valid_to)
SCD Type 3 (Previous value column)
quiz.expl: dbt snapshots capture changes in source records over time, inserting new versioned rows with dbt_valid_from and dbt_valid_to timestamps (classic SCD Type 2).

quiz.q: What is the difference between dbt seed and an ordinary data ingestion pipeline?
options: Seeds are small, version-controlled CSV files (like country code lookups) committed to the Git repo, not meant for large or frequently changing transactional data
Seeds can load petabyte-scale Parquet files directly from S3
Seeds bypass database authentication
Seeds are compiled into Python classes
quiz.expl: dbt seed loads small, static reference mappings (country codes, tax bands) stored directly in the repository; high-volume ingestion belongs in external ETL/ELT pipelines.

options: A table that is deleted automatically after 24 hours
A model that creates no physical relation in the database, but is injected as a Common Table Expression (CTE) into downstream models that reference it
A real-time Kafka streaming table
An unencrypted database view
quiz.expl: Ephemeral models do not create tables or views in the warehouse; dbt interpolates their SQL into referencing models as CTEs, keeping the warehouse namespace clean.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of Slim CI in a production dbt deployment?
options: To run dbt on micro-controllers
To build and test only the models modified in a Pull Request and their downstream dependents (state:modified+), using --defer to reference production relations for unmodified upstreams
To compress SQL code into minified files
To skip running tests entirely
quiz.expl: Slim CI dramatically reduces CI runtime and cloud warehouse cost by building only modified models and their downstream dependents, resolving unmodified parent models against production artifacts.

quiz.q: What command in dbt executes models, seeds, snapshots, and tests in their proper DAG dependency order?
options: dbt run
dbt compile
dbt build
dbt test
quiz.expl: dbt build is the unified command that executes seeds, models, snapshots, and tests in dependency order across the directed acyclic graph.

quiz.q: Why should a dbt model use a lookback window when filtering incremental updates?
options: To speed up query parsing
To capture late-arriving records whose update timestamps fall slightly behind the last recorded max timestamp
To prevent PostgreSQL from locking tables
To reduce database disk space
quiz.expl: A lookback window (e.g. updated_at >= max(updated_at) - INTERVAL '3 days') ensures records delayed by upstream network queues or out-of-order batches are not permanently skipped.
